title: The Vocabulary of Justifying Hurtful Comments
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article catalogs the verbal preambles leaders use to soften or justify comments they know will be hurtful, phrases like 'I'm just trying to help here' or 'tough love is never comfortable.' The author argues these justifications don't actually reduce the harm of what follows; instead, they create a psychological permission slip that makes leaders more likely to say increasingly inflammatory things over time. The piece describes this as a self-reinforcing cycle, since believing an excuse makes a comment more acceptable actually emboldens harsher language. The recommended fix is straightforward: if a leader catches themselves reaching for one of these justifying phrases, that's the signal to stop and not say the hurtful thing at all. Removing the excuse, the author argues, tends to remove the behavior itself.
points: Leaders often precede hurtful comments with justifying phrases meant to soften the impact
These preambles don't reduce harm; they function as permission to say something worse
The pattern is self-reinforcing, more excuses lead to more inflammatory comments over time
Catching yourself using a justifying phrase should be a signal to stop, not proceed
quotes: When a leader is about to say something hurtful, they often say things to make their actions sound more appropriate and reasonable.
The vocabulary of justifying hurtful comments is easy to spot because everyone uses them on occasion.
Leaders commonly believe that offering these preambles takes the edge off of what is going to be said or at least demonstrates that the speaker is not without self-awareness and some compassion.
Unfortunately, using such statements actually encourages more bad behavior in the future.
Ironically, because they believe these excuses and justifications make them appear more reasonable, their comments become more inflammatory.
Take the excuse away, and the behavior usually doesn’t occur. Work hard to change your vocabulary.
